Despite the disaster, she still got a NIPSCO bill for $374.</p><p>“It’s too much going on behind this power outage that we had to go through for two weeks,” she says. “It’s too much behind it. And the little that I’m going through, I could just imagine what other people are going through. I thought my home was safe. And now look: Me and my kids are truly sick.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/graphics/weather/powerless/12-nights-without-power-in-Gary-Indiana/" target="_blank" >12 nights without power in Gary</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/photography/2026/08/29/how-we-photographed-historic-power-outage-gary" >How we photographed a historic power outage in Gary</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-bb0000" name="module-bb0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h4><b>Resources for Gary residents: </b></h4><ul id="rte-8e577230-b2e0-11f1-b4e7-c913838dcc8d"><li>FEMA is accepting applications until Oct. 25, which can be filled out online at <a class="Link" href="https://www.disasterassistance.gov/" target="_blank" >www.disasterassistance.gov</a>. The federal agency provides funds to cover emergency needs, like medical equipment and food, and to make home repairs.</li><li>The Indiana State Disaster Relief Fund can help residents replace or repair essential furniture, appliances or pay for needed inspections. Residents can <a class="Link" href=" https://app.brightharbor.com/signup/indiana-sdrf-june-august-2026" target="_blank" >apply online</a>.</li><li>To get help in person applying for FEMA and the state’s relief fund, residents can visit United Steelworkers Local 1014, located at 1301 Texas St., Gary, Indiana, from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. from Sept. 23 to Sept. 25th. Residents can also stop by from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. on Sept. 28 through Oct. 2. The site will be part of the state’s “One-Stop Shops” to get state and federal disaster relief assistance.</li><li>To talk to a caseworker at the Red Cross, residents can call 1 (800) 733-2767.</li></ul><br><h4><b>How to help Gary residents: </b></h4><ul id="rte-8e577231-b2e0-11f1-b4e7-c913838dcc8d"><li>Tree of Life Missionary Baptist Church welcomes volunteers who want to help with relief efforts or their food pantry. They are located at 2323 W. 11th Ave., Gary, Indiana.</li><li>People interested in becoming a disaster volunteer with the Red Cross can visit, <a class="Link" href="https://redcross.org/volunteers" target="_blank" >redcross.org/volunteers</a>.</li><li>Hope Alliance of Northwest Indiana continues to distribute cleaning supplies and pays for residents to do loads of laundry. Volunteers interested in helping can call, (219) 316-0099.</li></ul></div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: After Tristan Peters' crash, do the White Sox need to rethink their outfield fences?
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> outfielder <b>Brenton Doyle </b>has a lot of respect for the way teammate <b>Tristan Peters </b>plays. Doyle just wishes that didn’t cost Peters on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/18/losing-ugly-sox-blow-big-early-lead-and-lose-to-tigers" target="_blank" >Friday night</a>, and doesn’t think it should have.</p><p>“I've had my fair share of those kind of hits against the wall,” Doyle said. “Honestly, it's a shame that they have outfield walls designed like that. I think they really need to lock into the safety of the players, especially for plays like that.”</p><p>During the fifth inning, Peters tried to chase down a <b>Kevin McGonigle </b>drive to right-center. Peters crashed into a padded stanchion supporting a see-through chain-link fence that’s in place so fans sitting in a patio area can watch the game.</p><p>Peters, who was out of the lineup Saturday but appeared to feel better than he did Friday, ended up with a left shoulder/rib contusion after the scary incident. Though it could be argued Peters got lucky considering the violence of the play, Doyle has a solution for avoiding repeats: get rid of the stanchions.</p><p>“If you have a flat surface wall like we have in left-center field, I don't think that happens, and I think he'd be able to play today,” Doyle said.</p><p>Making some switches, however, might bring its own complications. Even if the Sox would want to make changes it would take some engineering to maintain an unobstructed up-close view of the field while making things safer for the players.</p><p>But if something is tweaked before next season, it won’t be due to Sox manager <b>Will Venable</b>.</p><p>“There are a lot of things in every major-league ballpark that pose danger to players, that’s part of it,” Venable said. “As far as reevaluating the structure of our ballpark because of the play, that’s not my job.”</p><h2><b>A new experience</b></h2><p>Before his trade to the Sox, Doyle played the first three-plus years of his career with the Rockies and never came close to experiencing a playoff race.</p><p>Doyle said the excitement of playing for a postseason spot has “been a breath of fresh air.”</p><p>“This is the first time in my MLB career where I've actually paid attention to the division this late in the season,” Doyle said. “It's been exciting, keeping up with other games, and at the same time, feeling that pressure because I truly believe pressure is a privilege.”</p><h2><b>Bullpenning</b></h2><p>Sox starters are not providing much length, and that’s forcing Venable to find solutions to fill innings every day. With the playoff race coming down to the last games, Venable said navigating the bullpen is a “a journey every day and we’ll find what the path looks like.”</p><p>“It looks different every single day as different guys are available, you get different performances out of starters and you just kind of piece it together,” Venable said. “That’s been the daily challenge and part of finding ways to win every single game this season. That’s what every team’s doing every day. So that’s what we’ll continue to do.</p><p>Entering Saturday, Sox relievers had thrown 1 1/3 innings or more 202 times, tied with the 2024 Tigers for the second most in major-league history. The bullpen led baseball in innings pitched (726 2/3) and strikeouts (681).</p>

entries.title: 3 shot during argument in River North
entries.summary: <p>Three men were shot during an argument in River North early Saturday morning. </p><p>The men were outside in the 100 block of West Erie Street when they got in an argument with a person they did not know around 3:30 a.m., Chicago police said. </p><p>One man, 24, was shot in the leg and cheek, and was in critical condition, police said. </p><p>Another man, 25, was struck in both legs and the hand, while a third man, 22, was shot in both legs, police said. </p><p>All three men were in good condition and taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital. </p>

entries.title: Review: Iggy Pop still has a ‘lust for life’ in Riot Fest set to close out Day One
entries.summary: <p>Iggy Pop was the shirtless, fearless, ageless icon everyone had been waiting for on Friday night.</p><p>Baring his chest and a bit of his soul, the punk godfather whipped through a 13-song greatest hits set full of timeless favorites like “The Passenger” and “Raw Power” that have been a huge part of the backbone of an event like Riot Fest. It all made you wonder why he wasn’t on the main stage, yet just grateful he was there at all.</p><p>Iggy was up against Twenty One Pilots for the Friday finale spots, and the generational clash was obvious. There were too many bare pockets at Iggy Pop to feel excusable, but the ones who did show up were all but genuflecting. Good parents had kids on their shoulders to get a proper view. Most had their smartphones up in the air to grab videos for posterity’s sake. The loud group chanting of “I Wanna Be Your Dog” over and over even felt cult-like. Whether it was your first or 12th time seeing the legend, there was a mutual respect for the person who flipped the script on punk music — and has kept things interesting for more than 60 years.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-770000" name="image-770000"></a> <picture old. And while he may not be the untamed banshee he once was on stage, his approach was the same, preaching a message of living your life with unfettered abandon.</p><p>“I am not young, but once I was — and when I was a young man, I was in a band called The Stooges,” Iggy Pop said, dishing out a quick schooling on his proto-punk lineage before reaching into the archives for “1970.” It’s a song about being “young and alive,” he explained, putting umph into the song’s leading “woo!” chants. The vigor continued with the survivalist echoes of “Lust for Life,” with Iggy taking a quick crack at Trump and Putin before diving into the song that feels politically antithetical in 2026.</p><p>Iggy also took moments to make fun with the crowd, joking about needing a ride home ahead of “The Passenger” and wondering if the crowd wanted to do a group activity like a spa day or picnic or a “f------ ‘Death Trip’” to set up the rebel rant.</p><p>If his showmanship wasn’t enough, Iggy brought with him a solid backline of musicians including a three-piece horn section that added layered texture to each song, particularly the cacophony of the saxophone on “1969.” As the hourlong set wrapped, the punk stalwart bid adieu with goodbye waves and air kisses as the band played him out with “Funtime,” feeling like a directive for how to live your life.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/09/18/riot-fest-2026-violet-grohl-twenty-one-pilots-rise-against-weather-douglass-park-chicago-music" >Riot Fest 2026 kicks off with rising stars Violet Grohl, the Paradox and return of local punks Rise Against</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

and “Get out of our park!” on Saturday at Douglass Park. The British crooner behind The Smiths and a long solo career is notorious for canceling shows at the last minute.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The question of whether storms will pop up has often been overshadowed by another big “if”: Will Morrissey actually show? The British crooner behind The Smiths and a long solo career is notorious for canceling shows at the last minute — he just did so in August for a planned Vegas mini-residency. And while he has shown up for both of his previous Riot Fest appearances (in 2016 and 2021), he also has a contentious relationship with the event — in 2016, the staunch vegetarian even imposed a temporary “meat ban” for a two-hour window around his set, which continues to be a long-running inside joke for festivalgoers.</p><p>Over the past few weeks, local community groups have also voiced serious concern on social media over the singer’s planned appearance, citing Morrissey’s documented statements over the years related to UK immigration policies and his support of the far-right political party For Britain. Overnight, a large portion of covered fencing around the perimeters of Douglass Park was spray-painted with messages of “Racist Morrissey not welcome!” and “Get out of our park!”</p><p>If he doesn’t show, fans will have other options, with European punks Gogol Bordello and loudmouths Bad Religion performing during the same time frame. They’ll be followed by progressive metal rockers Tool and rapper Nas to close out the night, if the weather gods allow.</p><p>Read on for reviews of some of Saturday’s standout class="Figure-credit"><p>Ethan Chivari/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Aim High</h3><p>Aim High’s song “Flannel SZN” summed up the Chicago band’s feelings about opening the festivities for Riot Fest Day 2. “You'll come to find this is more than just a dream, this is everything to me,” sang front man Calebjustcaleb, closing his eyes for a moment to take it all in.</p><p>Just a few months ago, the singer relocated to Chicago from South Carolina and joined forces with local musicians in the North Lawndale neighborhood. They were chosen as one of Riot Fest’s four Community Bands of 2026, putting a spotlight on talent from the 24th Ward.</p><p> “We are extremely blessed to have the opportunity to play Riot Fest, especially a band of our size and being a newer local band to Chicago,” the singer told the Sun-Times in the press tent after Aim High’s set. “It’s a huge blessing and we very much appreciate the whole Riot Fest team and everyone who made it despite all the weather and us playing super early.”</p><p>“It’s amazing to be here,” said guitarist Cesar Leyva when the band was on stage. “Last year I was sitting in that f------ crowd with every single one of you,” he added, pointing out the commendable number of family and fans that showed up at noon in support of the band and/or keeping independent music alive in Chicago. </p><p>The five-piece bring a hearty blend of hardcore, alt-rock and pop punk on songs like “Here Lies Kakarot's Hopes & Dreams" with lyrics that talk about using “music as a vessel.” As Calebjustcaleb stood near the barricade to deliver the band’s final numbers to those gathered up front, he put that mission statement into action, uniting people of all walks of life in the same moment.</p><p>Aim High just released its latest EP “Free Caskets” in June, and hopefully there’s much more to come from them in the near future.</p>

entries.title: Review: Morrissey’s influence on legions of rockers, balladeers and goths is undeniable in Riot Fest set
entries.summary: <p>There was no long video delay, no meat ban to enact, no last-minute cancellation, just Morrissey with a tambourine in hand showing up and on time for his Riot Fest set in one of the most shocking moments of Saturday.</p><p>“I’m pleased to be here. I’m pleased to be alive. It’s a miracle,” the British singer said, nearly taking the words out of everyone’s mouths.</p><p>Due to impending inclement weather that prompted Riot Fest organizers and the city to cut festivities at 7 p.m. Saturday, Morrissey’s set was pushed up to 5:10 p.m. and reduced to 50 minutes — though he had a wise crack about that too. “The rain, the mud, the thunder, the lightning! We’re all gonna die,” he said as he played it off. “We have been warned we have to be very quick tonight, otherwise I’ll get my face kicked in, which I’m used to,” he cheekily added.</p><div Saturday’s appearance was no different, following a wave of controversy as local community groups chastised organizers for booking the controversial singer, who has a record of making statements about immigration and has been known to support right-wing movements. Overnight, fencing around Douglass Park was spray-painted with “racist Morrissey not welcome.”</p><p>In an interesting move, the singer started the set with images of civil rights icon James Baldwin, perhaps to counteract the sentiment. It also came minutes after Social Distortion ended its set with singer Mike Ness decrying racism as they played “Don’t Drag Me Down.” As Ness declared, “We believe immigrants make a country. White Christian nationalism isn’t going to fly.”</p><p>Even so, Morrissey chose to poke the bear with his comments. “Welcome to our soundcheck,” he joked about having a rushed set. “Can you hear us crystal clear? Is it disgusting?” The sizable crowd begged to differ with a dose of hearty applause. “I’m surprised,” he retorted.</p><p>What varnish this all leaves on his legacy is a conversation that would take more than 50 minutes and a few paragraphs to explore, but in the art vs. artist conversation, it would be hard to negate Morrissey’s influence on legions of rockers, balladeers and goths, ever obvious entries.title: Kevin Gausman's roller-coaster run with Cubs might be result of Blue Jays' World Series run
entries.summary: <p>CINCINNATI — Veteran right-hander Kevin Gausman has been riding a roller coaster since joining the Cubs before the trade deadline. It’s not one he’s enjoying.</p><p>“It’s really frustrating,” Gausman told the Sun-Times, “especially after being really consistent for the last five, six years.”</p><p>Gausman has alternated good and bad outings for weeks, going from seven innings of scoreless ball to four innings with six runs, including three home runs. In eight starts for the Cubs, Gausman has a 5.04 ERA.</p><p>In his previous five seasons, one with the Giants and four with the Blue Jays, Gausman had a 3.34 ERA in 158 starts. With 2,083 innings on his arm in 14 regular seasons, he knows he’s dealing with wear and tear, and it isn’t easy.</p><p>“You’ve got to give yourself a little bit of grace when it comes to the workload that I had last year,” Guasman said. “My 13th year, I made it to the World Series. So for 12 years, I had one way of doing the offseason. I’ve been in a lot of postseasons but never made it very far.”</p><p>In his first 12 seasons, Gausman totaled 25 ⅔ innings in the postseason. Last year during the Jays’ run to the World Series, he totaled 30 ⅔. In 2024, a non-playoff year, Gausman began his offseason throwing regimen on Oct. 28, the same day as Game 3 of the World Series. In 2025, he started Games 2 and 6 of the World Series.</p><p>“So I threw for over a year, threw the most pitches in all of baseball, most starts in all of baseball, most innings,” Gausman said. “So with that and less time, it was tricky trying to figure out how I make sure that I’m ready for the start of this season while also giving myself a little bit of a break. I came to the realization that I just wasn’t going to have much of a break.”</p><p>He might be feeling that now. After all, Gausman’s season with the Jays wasn’t rosy, either. He had a 4.38 ERA in 23 starts. Knowing the load he carried last season, the Jays had him build back up slowly in spring training. But as Gausman said, there’s no manual to help a pitcher prepare for the season after a World Series run.</p><p>“It’s hard to tell whether it was last year or just a combination of my whole career,” he said.</p><p>Cubs manager Craig Counsell said another factor is at play: Gausman is basically a two-pitch pitcher, fastball and splitter.</p><p>“It puts a higher premium on his execution,” Counsell said. “The hitter’s got two pitches to think about. He’s paid for his mistakes a little bit more. But when you’re relying on those two pitches, that kind of makes sense.</p><p>“The split-finger is also more difficult to throw, but when you get it going, it’s really hard to hit. When it’s not going your way, you’re probably going to throw balls with it. And he’s two pitches, so there’s not another pitch to go to.”</p><p>Which begs the question: How will the Cubs use Gausman in the postseason? They acquired him with his postseason experience in mind, but he might not get a start in the wild-card series. He doesn’t know what his role will be in the playoffs.</p><p>“I don’t think anybody knows,” Gausman said. “Nobody knew Chris Bassit was going to throw [8 ⅔] innings out of the [Jays’] bullpen in the World Series and only give up one run. It’s going to take every single guy on this staff to do what we want to do, which is go to the World Series.</p><p>“It’s all hands on deck. I’ve pitched out of the bullpen in the postseason. If you’ve been starting all year, it’s different. But you’ve just got to go into it with the mentality that it’s going to take everybody, and if you tell them you’re fresh, the phone might ring and it might be you.”</p>

entries.title: Goode's ground attack cruises past Brooks
entries.summary: <p>It’s a pass-happy era in high school football, with the state career-yardage record going down each of the last two seasons. But Goode has found a different path to success.</p><p>The Knights run the ball more than 90% of the time and have a seemingly endless supply of running backs. The ringleader is junior quarterback Jordan Boston, whose deception keeps defenses guessing — usually wrong.</p><p>Saturday was a typical day at the office for Goode, which cruised to a 60-20 victory against visiting Brooks while using nine ball carriers.</p><p>Aedan Cleveland carried 11 times for 192 yards and three touchdowns, ran a punt back 75 yards for a fourth score and caught a pass for 28 yards.</p><p>Boston ran for 113 yards and a touchdown — also on 11 carries — and completed two of his three passes for 51 yards and a touchdown.</p><p>Caron Williams added three carries for 56 yards and a touchdown, and Gabriel Chambers-Crosby also had a touchdown run.</p><p>‘‘Our thing is, if you can play, you’re going to play,’’ Knights coach Terrence McClarn said. ‘‘We want as many guys [as possible] to get reps, and that keeps our guys fresh.’’</p><p>Cleveland, who led the team in rushing last season, is fine with spreading the wealth.</p><p>‘‘I like to get my rest, and I like to get other people their attention, too,’’ he said.</p><p>One of those people Saturday was 5-10, 281-pound senior tight end Trenell Clark.</p><p>‘‘Freshman year, he was a center,’’ McClarn said. ‘‘Then he got moved to tackle. And then he was playing catch and things. . . . [In] our offense, we need a tight end who can block.’’</p><p>Clark does that and more.</p><p>‘‘His hands [are] just out of this world,’’ McClarn said. ‘‘And he can move for a big fella.’’</p><p>Clark made a one-handed catch of a 23-yard scoring pass — his first career touchdown — and also ran once for nine yards.</p><p>How did he take the news that he would be a full-time tight end?</p><p>‘‘It felt great that I was going to be a part of the skill players and build more chemistry with them,’’ Clark said.</p><p>Goode (3-1, 2-0 Red Southwest) has had an unusual season. The Knights forfeited to T.F. North because of low numbers and other issues in Week 2, then had a no contest against Orr in Week 3 when the Public League schedule was jumbled because of the heat advisory.</p><p>The Knights’ victory last week against Hyde Park ended a 22-day gap between games.</p><p>‘‘We’ve still got to clean up the mistakes,’’ McClarn said. ‘‘I’d be happy if we stopped fumbling the ball. So ball security, make sure we take care of the ball. We’re getting there.’’</p><p>Junior Antoine Mathis led Brooks (2-3, 0-2) with six carries for 85 yards, including a 39-yard touchdown. Mathis started the season at defensive back and just moved to offense last week.</p><p>Eagles coach Clifford Brisseus is in his second season. He said a big focus has been on changing the mindset in a program whose last winning season was 2021.</p><p>‘‘It’s that mentality change,’’ Brisseus said. ‘‘It’s way better than last year. So every year, you improve and improve and improve.’’</p>

entries.title: Bridgeport and Chinatown residents press Amtrak leaders to 'pump the brakes' on rail yard plan
entries.summary: <p>Amtrak officials and developers faced off against angry community members Thursday, opposing construction plans for a massive rail yard in Chinatown, Bridgeport and Armour Square beginning as early as the end of this year.</p><p>The plan, headed by Amtrak and White Sox minority owner <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2025/06/06/justin-ishbia-white-sox-jerry-reinsdorf-ownership-winnetka" target="_blank" ><u>Justin Ishbia’s</u></a> company, Canal Edge LLC, works alongside a proposal for the Sox to play at a mixed-use facility along the Chicago River called The Railyards in the South Loop. Under the proposal, Amtrak’s maintenance facility would move into the neighborhood on South Canal Street between West 33rd and 35th streets.</p><p>Hundreds of residents, some dressed in T-shirts that read “Protect our community, stop Amtrak’s rail yard,” flooded the meeting. Tensions rose as Amtrak leaders and developers claimed there were no significant impacts on the environment or quality of life for nearby residents housed near the proposed site.</p><p>Residents responded by questioning the studies Amtrak has done regarding impacts on safety, the environment, noise and other factors. The project has received $600 million and a categorical exclusion from the federal government to bypass certain environmental tests and an environmental impact statement to break ground faster, but residents also questioned that.</p><p>“You’re treating us like we’re idiots. We’re not idiots,” one resident said. “We’re intelligent, hardworking people making our home here.”</p><p>Steven Segerlin, who runs commercial development at Amtrak, said the company needs a new site for a rail yard to replace its current 14th Street facility. The revamped site would allow the company to modernize its maintenance, cleaning and storage practices, allowing for fewer delays.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: King beats Simeon: 'We run the Red, and we run Chicago.'
entries.summary: <p>King’s large, athletic linemen sacked Simeon quarterback Aki King on back-to-back downs midway through the fourth quarter.</p><p>Then seniors Damare Griffin (6-4, 305 pounds), Cornelius Moore (6-6, 230), Denero Jenkins (6-2, 330) and Prince McGill (6-0, 275) switched over to the offensive side of the ball and created a hole that may change the course of King football history.</p><p>Senior running back Herman Yancey blasted through it for a 55-yard touchdown run, giving the Jaguars their first lead against Simeon in many years.</p><p>“I was patient, and I waited for the hole to open up and then exploded and scored,” Yancey said.</p><p>Yancey rushed for 135 yards and two touchdowns in the Jaguars’ 19-16 win against Simeon on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/scores/2026/09/17/high-school-football-scores-week-5" >Saturday</a> at Stagg Stadium.</p><p>His second TD came with 2:57 left and provided enough of a cushion for King to withstand a 95-yard kickoff return touchdown by star Simeon sophomore Jalonny Billingsley a few seconds later.</p><p>“It is real,” Wolverines coach Sinque Turner said. “King is here. I have to give them their roses. You can’t take anything away from what they did on this football field. I take my cap off to them. This is a tough loss. A very, very tough loss.”</p><p>The game's intensity was too high for most of the first half. Both sides committed personal fouls, and it was a sloppy, penalty-filled slog.</p><p>“We’ve been talking about it being a dogfight all week,” King coach Abdullah Asad. “The first half, there were a lot of penalties. That’s a good football team, and we are a good football team. But we made some great adjustments and kept things under control in the second half.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure and a one-yard TD run from James Bell right before halftime.</p><p>King’s first score came on a 10-yard touchdown pass from Tremaine Ford to Emmanuel James late in the third quarter.</p><p>“It was very intense,” Moore said. “It felt like a college game. I was very excited going into this week, and we did great, and we finished. It is a statement piece. We run the Red, and we run Chicago.”</p><p>Bell had 16 carries for 74 yards for Simeon. King went 6-for-15, throwing for 102 yards with two interceptions.</p><p>“There were some bad decisions on our end and a lack of execution,” Turner said. “We beat ourselves. King’s coaching staff is doing a phenomenal job. Those are guys that are close to me, and they coached their butts off today. They shut us out in the second half. I have to give them their credit.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Herman Yancey breaks loose for a 55-yard TD. <br><br>King stuffed Simeon with back to back sacks to get the ball. <br><br>Jaguars lead Simeon 12-8 with 9:21 left. <a href="https://t.co/m6df1C5BvL">pic.twitter.com/m6df1C5BvL</a></p>— Michael O'Brien (@michaelsobrien) <a href="https://x.com/michaelsobrien/status/2101401060065624180?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 19, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>King (4-1, 2-0) knocked off St. Laurence earlier this season, and its only loss is to Marist. Close observers of Public League football knew it was a program on the rise, but there was no concrete proof until Saturday.</p><p>“It is a full circle moment for me for sure,” Asad said. “I’ve been coaching in CPS for eight years, and everybody always tells me what I couldn’t do. I said when I got my guys, we would be good to go. A lot of these guys that are seniors right now have been with the program for three or four years. They are drinking the Kool-Aid and doing a great job.”</p><p>Simeon has played a challenging schedule, but has high expectations for the season. Next up for the Wolverines is a showdown with rival Morgan Park.</p><p>“We will see what these guys are made of, if they can dust themselves off and get ready for Morgan Park,” Turner said. “That is going to be a heck of a game. Those guys are going to come for blood. We have to do some soul searching in our camp.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-250000" name="html-embed-module-250000"></a><blockquote class="tiktok-embed" cite="https://www.tiktok.com/@michaelsobriensports/video/7687373529708301598" data-video-id="7687373529708301598" style="max-width: 605px;min-width: 325px;" > <section> <a target="_blank" title="@michaelsobriensports" href="https://www.tiktok.com/@michaelsobriensports?refer=embed">@michaelsobriensports</a> King’s line was dominant on both sides of the ball in the win against Simeon. <a title="ihsa" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/ihsa?refer=embed">#ihsa</a> <a title="football" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/football?refer=embed">#football</a> <a title="chicago" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/chicago?refer=embed">#chicago</a> <a target="_blank" title="♬ original sound - michaelsobriensports" href="https://www.tiktok.com/music/original-sound-7687373558565096223?refer=embed">♬ original sound - michaelsobriensports</a> </section> </blockquote> <script async src="https://www.tiktok.com/embed.js"></script> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Miguel Vargas, Sean Burke lead White Sox to crucial 3-1 win over Tigers
entries.summary: <p>Just hours removed from a crushing loss with severe playoff implications, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> needed their best players to deliver.</p><p>The Sox got that Saturday from third baseman Miguel Vargas and starting pitcher Sean Burke in a 3-1 win over the Tigers. On Friday, they <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/18/losing-ugly-sox-blow-big-early-lead-and-lose-to-tigers" >squandered an 8-2 lead</a> and lost 11-8, and because Saturday’s game was moved to the afternoon due to a stormy forecast, the Sox had little time to stew over a crushing defeat and risk losing more ground to the Guardians in the divisional race or competitors for the AL wild card.</p><p>As he’s been all season, Vargas was a reason the Sox successfully moved on. He hit his 33rd home run in the sixth inning and scored on a Munetaka Murakami single in the first to become the first Sox player to score 100 runs, homer and double 30 times and steal 20 bases in a season.</p><p>“That's why I wake up every day and work so hard for these types of moments,” Vargas said. “It's just this group has been pushing me every single day. And I never have been thinking about my individual stats, I just want to go out there and do the best for my team, and have some fun and always try hard.”</p><p>Vargas’ contributions didn’t stop on offense. To end the Tigers’ fourth, he snagged a sharp Dillon Dingler grounder to preserve the Sox’ 1-0 lead.</p><p>“He’s been awesome,” Burke said. “Even down the stretch, he’s turned it up another notch on both sides of the ball, which is huge to see.”</p><p>The Sox were hoping for the same from Burke, and he gave them something they hadn’t had in almost a month.</p><p>He threw six innings and gave up a run, producing the Sox’ first quality start since Burke’s on Aug. 21 against the Mets. The outing wasn’t always pretty – Burke walked three and said his day was “a little grindy” – but it was enough and lowered his ERA over his last 17 outings to 2.80.</p><p>“One of those days where you really need him to step up and have a good outing and cover a lot of innings and give us a chance to win,” manager Will Venable said. “I thought he did a great job.”</p><p>Venable and the Sox’ coaching staff helped, too.</p><p>Holding a 2-1 lead with two outs in the top of the sixth, Burke loaded the bases. On a 2-1 count, Detroit’s Brett Callahan swung through a pitch that eluded Sox catcher Kyle Teel, bringing in the tying run. But Venable and the Sox challenged the play, saying the pitch hit Callahan, which would then make the ball dead.</p><p>The Sox won the challenge, taking the run away from the Tigers. Burke then struck out Callahan to keep the Sox in front.</p><p>“It’s almost like getting another life back and kind of just seeing that happen and knowing that I’ve got another chance to keep this thing in our favor and keep the lead,” Burke said. “Once that happens, it’s just bearing down and making a pitch.”</p><p>The Sox will have to do the same to win the division or earn a wild card spot. There have been hiccups and moments that cast reasonable doubt on this young team’s ability to do that, but on Saturday they rebounded from perhaps their worst moment of the season.</p><p>“This is what this team is about. We never give up,” Vargas said. “We always come back and battle the next day and play all nine innings. That's what we have been doing the whole year, just show up that day.”</p>

entries.title: Illini pound Salukis ahead of their Ohio State showdown next week
entries.summary: <p>CHAMPAIGN— Katin Houser threw two second-quarter touchdown passes to Collin Dixon to lead Illinois past Southern Illinois 48-10 on Saturday.</p><p>Dixon caught eight passes for 131 yards for the Illini (2-1), who opened the season with three home games. Dixon has seven TD catches, already the single-season record at Gies Memorial Stadium with four home games remaining.</p><p>“Collin's start is incredible,” said Illinois coach Bret Bielema. “He's extremely talented, so humble, and he works his absolute (backside) off every day. He's really special.”</p><p>Hudson Clement had five catches for 69 yards for Illinois. He’s caught a pass in 30 straight games, the sixth-longest active streak in the nation.</p><p>Houser was 23-of-29 passing for 305 yards. He was intercepted once.</p><p>Aiden Laughery ran for 93 yards on four carries and scored a TD for Illinois.</p><p>One play after Houser was sacked for the first time this season, Laughery ran 77 yards down the Illinois sideline for a TD that put the Illini ahead for good 14-7 late in the first quarter. It was the longest run for the Illini in five years.</p><p>D.J. Williams was 20-of-38 passing for Southern Illinois (2-2). He was in the running last season for the Walter Payton Award, presented to the best player in the Championship Subdivision.</p><p>Matthew Bailey picked off an overthrown Williams pass and ran 88 yards for a TD in the fourth quarter.</p><p>Williams was held to 7 yards rushing on seven attempts after running for four TDs last week in a win over Southeast Missouri. The Salukis had just 29 yards on the ground against Illinois.</p><p>“There were some good moments, but the bottom line is we just got beat 48-10, so it should be a quiet locker room,” said Southern Illinois coach Nick Hill. “Now it's time for (Missouri Valley Football Conference) play and they all matter.”</p><p><b>The Takeaway</b></p><p>Illinois did a better job tackling and running the ball than it did in its first two games, but has it improved enough in those areas as it heads into Big Ten play? It was difficult to tell facing an FCS opponent, but encouraging nonetheless.</p><p>After forcing just a dozen turnovers last season, Southern Illinois had eight going into the Illinois game including four interceptions last week against Southeast Missouri. The Salukis had to add a few more to their turnover total if they were going to have a shot to beat the Illini and they came up with just one, an end zone interception by Sebastian Vargas in the third quarter.</p><p><b>FCS domination</b></p><p>Illinois is now 21-0 vs. FCS teams since the division was formed in 1978. Bielema is 4-0, with the Illini outscoring those teams 176-13. Southern Illinois received a reported $525,000 to play in Champaign.</p><p><b>Road warriors</b></p><p>Southern Illinois plays four of its first five games and seven of its 12 games on the road this season, but the Salukis are normally no slouches away from Carbondale. They were at least .500 in road games four times in the last five years.</p><p><b>8 TDs vs. Southern Illinois</b></p><p>Former Illinois star and two-time Super Bowl champion Howard Griffith ran for an NCAA record eight touchdowns in the Illini’s 56-21 win over Southern Illinois in 1990.</p><p><b>Up next</b></p><p>Illinois: At No. 6 Ohio State next Saturday.</p><p>Southern Illinois: At Murray State next Saturday.</p>
entries.author: AP

entries.title: Man critically injured after falling onto CTA Blue Line tracks in West Loop, police say
entries.summary: <p>A 39-year-old man was critically injured early Saturday when he fell from a CTA Blue Line platform onto the tracks and was struck by an oncoming train in the West Loop, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The incident occurred at 5:55 a.m. along the 400 block of South Clinton Street near the Clinton station, police said.</p><p>The man was taken to Stroger Hospital in critical condition, according to police.</p><p>No further information was available.<br></p>
